description: Richard Avila, deported at 56 after living in East Los Angeles since he was two, described Tijuana as feeling like being sent to the moon - not American, not Mexican, in bicultural limbo, where the way he spoke put a target on his back. Colleagues at the maquiladora called him pocho, a derogatory term for a Mexican who left.
energy_note: Foreign in the country of his own passport.

description: One shelter worker described the disorientation directly: having grown up over there, not knowing the culture, feeling awkward about how he speaks and looks, because people can tell he is not from there. He has seen deportees without support become homeless, develop substance problems, or end up in prison.
energy_note: Asked to become a nationality he already legally is.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the criminal-record stigma travels with him
description: One call centre worker, Omar, asked that his surname not be used because of the stigma attached to deported convicts in Mexico, describing 21 years in prison and deportation three years earlier.
energy_note: Anonymous in his own country, about his own past.

aspect: EXAMPLE - and the accent becomes the only asset
description: Tijuana's call centres grew from roughly 10 to more than 60 in two decades, most employing deportees, drawing work away from India on accent-neutral English at Mexican wages - 'Tijuana has become like the new Bombay,' per a recruiter of 16 years. Avila called it the best possible job for a deportee: better paid than construction or the maquiladora, and the first place his English was an asset rather than a scarlet letter.
money_note: Approx. monthly call centre pay, USD.
energy_note: The thing that marked him became the thing that paid him.

description: The tattoo-as-gang-marker barrier is widely described anecdotally, and targeted searching did not surface sourced documentation of it as an employment barrier for deportees. Recorded as unverified rather than asserted.
energy_note: Everyone says it; nothing sourced found.

aspect: The word he uses for where he is from is now wrong in both places
description: Saying 'back home' in Tijuana means Los Angeles, and saying it in Los Angeles meant Michoacán. There is no sentence he can say about home that is not confusing to whoever is listening.
energy_note: No way to finish the sentence 'back home'.
